Circumcision: Search for identity

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
An English father, a Xhosa mother the story of Litha's search for identity and a rare insight into traditional circumcision.

Summary:
Litha is 18 years old and he can't seem to find where he fits in culturally. His doesn't see himself as white black or coloured. He became depressed and even had to go onto medication. Then his parents started exploring his cultural identity to try and find meaning in his heritage. The circumcision ritual stood out as a rite of passage and Litha signed up in December. In a rare deviation from the secrecy of the ritual we were allowed to film every step of the way including the moment of circumcision and the "coming out" held in the suburbs where racial and cultural differences were shrugged off the suburban lawns where his Xhosa mother and his white girlfriend sat alongside elders and neighbours in a show of tolerance and acceptance in the true spirit of the rainbow nation.

It's what we expect in the coming of age of our country - we need more stories like this one.

Tim Hewitt-Coleman Litha's dad and architect
Hlubi Coleman Litha's mom
Amber Litha's girlfriend
Luzuko Buyambo Litha' caretaker during the initiation

Press Release:


Choosing circumcision
As the son of an English father and a Xhosa mother, Litha Coleman doesn’t see himself as black, white or coloured. In search of meaning, heritage and a cultural identity, he shares rare insight into his decision to be circumcised through traditional Xhosa rituals. Carte Blanche follows his journey, every step of the way.


Script:


Script – Coming of Age


VO: 10”
In 1993 with the country on the threshold of its new democracy Hlubi and Tim’s love story was seen as symbolic of the sweeping changes in the country at the time.


Tim:
We were flavor of the month because we were, in our group, reflecting thatnew South Africa that people were speaking about.


Hlubi: 17:
I saw Tim as just a normal person, just a human being, I didn’t see colour because that is not how I was brought up.

Tim:
I’d like to make up a story and say how hard it was and how we struggled and fought off these racists and everything but actually it really wasn’t like that.


VO: 5
Hlube’s mom, Thami, who was a domestic worker, needed some convincing.


Thami:
Yo I said I am not happy about it. He said why, I said you know what I don’t trust for the white man to marry my daughter.


VO: 4”
But Tim soon won her over and the wedding went ahead.


John:
And then as Tim says, you settled down and had children?

Hlubi:
It was very exciting, we were all looking forward to see this baby, how he’s going to look, it was amazing.

VO: 5
When baby Litha was born there was much celebration but also some tough decisions


Circumcision link
To circumcise or not to circumcise, that was the question faced by Tim and Hlubi’s whose cultures offered two very different and competing answers. At birth in Tim’s case or in the teenage year’s in Hlubi’s.


Tim:
Well that was our first cop out in our relationship, that was one of the first major things that we had to decide. And we had a discussion and so we had a discussion and like all good politicians, not that we are politicians, when we can’t reach a decision today we postpone it for a long time and so we reached a compromise and we said let Litha decide when he’s an adult, when he’s 18.


VO: 5”
As Litha grewp he straddled two cultures and carved out his own identity.


Litha:
I never really wanted to be that person are you black or are you white? tI’ve kind of just been myself, but if people ask me I make a joke and say today I feel like being black, so that’s what I am today and maybe tomorrow I will be white.


VO:10”
Litha spent a lot of time in the townships with his grandmother and there it was expected of him to go through with the traditional Xhosa initiation rights and circumcision – if he didn’t he’d always be considered a boy and not a man in that world.

Litha:
They say, ja we’ll go to your mngidi when you turn 18, when are you going to the bush, so its always been in that culture I’m going to be going to the bush.


Tim:
Other boys they’d be able to rest back and say I don’t really have a choice. My father will never let me not got, so in a way I think we made things more difficult for Litha because we said look its your choice we will support you whichever way. You can pull out any time.


VO: 3”
But Litha kept to his resolve.


Thami:
He said to me you know Makhulu I want to go to the bush and I said you Litha there’s no white person that is going to the bush, he said Makhulu I am going to the bush.


VO: 3”
This despite his girlfriend Amber’s reservations.


Amber:
When he said to me that he was going was a bit like why do you want to go? But I supported him.

VO: 6”
So the search became for an inkangata or traditional doctor to perform the operation safely.


Tim:
Our headlines in our province are full of young boys dying in this process of circumcision.


VO: 7”
Mthembu Mondi says he was honoured when they asked him to be both inkangata and umnibi – doctor and nurse.


Mthembu:
You are dealing with a person, you are dealing with a life. You know those young boys are the leaders of tomorrow. You must be careful when you are doing this job.

VO: 16”
So in early December they gathered and built an iboma as a shelter for Litha on an uninhabited farm owned by the family. His father Tim helped prepare him on day one in preparation of the circumcision rites. As custom demands they shaved his head, stripped him naked and dressed in just a blanket as he waited for the surgeon to mark the beginning of the 3 week ritual.


Litha:
I honestly I was never really nervous or scared.

VO:
Tim was a different story.


Mthembu:
I said to Tim I think that Litha is a little bit nervous and he said to me no it’s me who is nervous!


VO: 16”
The initiation rites are usually shrouded in secrecy but Litha’s family allowed our cameras to capture a rare insight into the traditional Xhosa practice. Mthembu had performed the operation many times before and he positioned Litha next to his iboma.

Mthembu
“Your’s, panicking, look at me…Just relax.”

VO
No anasthetic is given and using a short traditional spear Mthembu deftly sliced off the foreskin - in a matter of seconds it was all over.

Upsound!!!
Yizo yizo yizo!


Tim:
It was difficult, but it was enriching, enlivening. I felt alive doing it. On the day that Litha was circumcised, I had to stand there and I had to watch my child being cut. It was difficult for me, it was heavy but this is what we have to do, something that we have chosen to do that we now have got to carry through with.

VO: 9”
The first week is considered the most critical time – apart from the pain and healing Litha had to follow time honoured protocols. He is covered in clay which according to folklore serves a double purpose - to keep him clean, as he’s not allowed to wash and to ward off snakes.


Tim:
For the first week all you have a blanket, that’s all you have, and that’s very difficult also because the Xhosa tradition is that your food intake is very limited, basically dry food, boiled mealies and very little water.

John:

It’s almost worse than the circumcision?

Litha:
Jeez yes that was the worst part - the diet!

VO: 11”
Equally difficult for a modern teenager was having no smartphone or access to the outside world. His uncle Luzuko Buyambo volunteered to stay with his initiate nephew as a caretaker and to show him the ropes.

Luzuko:
I also told him from my experience, this is the way of life, this is the way you must act as a man.

VO: 13”
With Luzuko’s guidance Litha spent those first few days going through the traditional Xhosa rituals – making a stick that he will carry with him into manhood for the rest of his life. He also found time to mull over why he found his father’s heritage unappealling.

Litha:
And I said Dad tell me about your ancestors and your traditions and he said my ancestors are Irish and they found potatoes…and that was it.

VO: 10”
His healing happened fast and on day 8 Litha was given a clean bill of health. To mark the occasion the men of the family gathered and in keeping with tradition they slaughtered a goat.


Tim:
Why are we here today we are here today to eat some meat meat today for the first time in a week, he’s able to have some salt with his meat and something spicy, something tasty and that’s it.


VO: 5”
The two weeks that followed were more of a retreat… a time of self reflection.


Litha:
If I have a son, I’ll do the same that my parents did, I’ll leave the decision up to him. Because look I have a black mother so I have the decision to either go the black way or the white way. I won’t be a black father to my child, I’m only half.


Tim:
He just looks so much more radiant, he looks so much more calm and in control and I think that simply had to do with, if I were asked to theorise,just the fact that there was a retreat.


VO: 17
His time in the bush was soon over and again the men gathered at his iboma to complete the ritual. First they washed Litha and rubbed butter all over his body. Then they wrapped him in a new blanket, together with his helper or Iqalathi who will journey home with him. He then turns his back on his iboma as the men set it alight.


Tim:
Symbolically as the man leaves the bush you burn this structure behind him this iboma, with all his clothes so symbolically you are burning his childhood


John link
After three weeks Litha returned from the bush having completed his rite of passage. Only one more ceremony awaited after which his family and friends could eat, drink, sing and dance.


VO: 6”
The women waited on his street in Port Elizabeth’s upmarket suburb of Walmer for Litha to arrive.

Litha:
You have to stand with that blanket and the woman can’t see you yet until the men have said they can see you so its serious face.

Thami:
Prospect road, hey! It was full of people and we were happy singing ubiyele, ubiyele,….

VO: 7”
Hlubi battled to contain herself and leapt into the air in delight. Amber recalls being very emotional.



Amber:
I remember I got so choked up and I had to look away and my jaw got so sore from clenching it trying not to cry.


VO: 6”
He was welcomed back as a man by the elders who put a lot of pressure on him.


Elder: party 2

Litha now you have reached manhood now. You can be an example of what we want of the children to come in this country. You can go anywhere now and say I am African.

VO: 5”
After the civilities Litha was taken to him room where first his sister Mandisa.
And then his friends and girlfriends coated him in clay – it’s the way the women welcome him back as a new man.

VO:
What followed was probably one of the biggest parties Walmer has ever seen – 350 people joined in the celebration as Litha left his childhood behind him.


Tim:
Now that I am the father of man, I am a man in a way I wasn’t before, so it definitely is a big important chapter in our lives.


Promos

Promo 1

VO: 10”
A love story that transcends race….their son’s decision to follow in the footsteps of his Xhosa ancestors. We celebrate a right of passage with a remarkable Port Elizabeth family.


Promo 2”

VO: 6”
A rare insight into traditional Xhosa initiation rights as we join Litha Hewitt Coleman on his journey to manhood.

Thami:
Yo Litha there’s no white man that goes to the bush.

VO: 4
It’s a story of hope at a time of simmering racial tensions.



Promo 3:

VO: 7
If you’re born to a Xhosa family the traditional circumcision ritual is an important part of any boy’s journey to manhood – even if you’re only half Xhosa.

Litha:
It’s always been there that I am going to the bush.

VO: 4
And his father supports him every step of the way.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): An English father, a Xhosa mother the story of Litha's search for identity and a rare insight into traditional circumcision.
metadata.Summary: Litha is 18 years old and he can't seem to find where he fits in culturally. His doesn't see himself as white black or coloured. He became depressed and even had to go onto medication. Then his parents started exploring his cultural identity to try and find meaning in his heritage. The circumcision ritual stood out as a rite of passage and Litha signed up in December. In a rare deviation from the secrecy of the ritual we were allowed to film every step of the way including the moment of circumcision and the "coming out" held in the suburbs where racial and cultural differences were shrugged off the suburban lawns where his Xhosa mother and his white girlfriend sat alongside elders and neighbours in a show of tolerance and acceptance in the true spirit of the rainbow nation. It's what we expect in the coming of age of our country - we need more stories like this one.
